features.name: Term usage detection and promotion to context
Dual-language safety case content
features.notes: Per-element `name_langs` / `content_langs` maps carried through the model. A name carrying more than one language does not fit clause 8.6, so import parks the extra languages in a reserved `sacm.import.name` TaggedValue and the projection recombines them. That recombination used to let an overflow entry with no `lang` claim the primary's slot, replacing an English claim name with its translation on every projection — which changed what the claim asserted, made the canonical hash unstable, and left affected projects reporting an audit divergence that Reconcile could not clear. The overflow now never overwrites the primary language, and repeated project/serialize cycles are asserted to converge rather than accumulate.

features.name: Register assessments persist with the project
features.notes: Owners, criteria, assessment status and notes are held by `RegisterController`, saved to `registers/register-assessments.af.json` on project save, and tracked in the manifest. A file that fails to load is reported in the register tab, editing is disabled and saving is refused, so a bad read cannot overwrite what is on disk. Only rows a user edited are stored. An assessment whose CSE or evidence id leaves the argument is kept, never auto-deleted, and raised as a warning in the Problems panel carrying the stored content — the row is gone from the table, so the problem is the only place left to read it. Its "Discard assessment" quick fix drops it in memory; the file is only rewritten on save, so closing without saving takes it back.

features.name: MCP server — read a safety case from an external AI client
features.notes: Design: docs/features/mcp-server.md. `assurance-forge-mcp` speaks JSON-RPC 2.0 over stdio and reads a case (overview, search, element detail, GSN tree, argument files). It runs in one of two modes. **Connected**: Assurance Forge has the project open, and every operation is answered by the application over the local bridge (AF-AI-008), from the argument the user is looking at including unsaved edits. **Offline**: no application is running, so the adapter loads its own copy — and is read-only, because changing a safety case needs a command bus, an audit log and a human to accept it. Both modes execute the same `src/agent/` implementations, so an agent does not get different answers depending on whether a window is open. Consent: ADR 0007, a flag that fails closed, re-read on every call so revocation takes effect immediately, and verified through the real process by cmake/run_mcp_smoke_test.cmake. Independent of AF-AI-001..006: the layer gate forbids `mcp/` from including `ai/`.

features.name: Local bridge between the MCP adapter and the running application
features.notes: A versioned, user-private, message-framed connection: Windows named pipe, POSIX AF_UNIX socket, no TCP. The application publishes one endpoint record per open project in the user's runtime directory — never in the project, which keeps `af.proj` under a single writer. Two gates: the operating system's access control on the pipe, and a 256-bit token from that record. **Requests execute on the frame thread**, so an operation sees exactly the model the user sees and needs no lock. Every frame carries a protocol version, and a mismatch between an old adapter and a newer application is reported as one message naming both versions. Both platform branches are compiled in CI; the Windows branch was additionally built with MinGW g++ and the POSIX branch with GCC 15.2.

features.name: Propose changes to a safety case from an external AI client
features.notes: An agent builds a **change set** the user watches take shape: from its first staged operation the GSN canvas draws the argument as it would be if accepted, with additions, edits and removals marked in place by border and badge (never colour alone). **A change set belongs to the argument file it was written against.** Element ids repeat across a project's arguments — each is seeded from the same template, so each starts with the same top goal — so without that binding a change set built against one argument decorated another's identically-named elements, and Accept refused with a staleness message that named the wrong cause. Staging, submitting and accepting are all refused while a different argument is open, and the Review panel says which one to open. Staging changes nothing — no SACM write, no command, no audit transaction — and a change set that would not apply is refused at staging time, so the canvas can always draw one. **Acceptance is an ordinary audited edit**: it goes through the unchanged `ApplyProposalCommand`, so it is undoable, replayable and attributed to the connecting client -- the transaction author reads `MCP: <client>`, verified by accepting in the running application and reading the log, which is the only place that wiring shows. No agent-specific command type exists, which is what guarantees an agent cannot make a change the application could not make itself. Staleness is re-checked at acceptance, not at staging, because the user may edit the argument while reading the proposal — against the model the patch produces, so a change set that develops its own earlier creations by the id `stage_operations` reported for them still accepts. Checking references against the committed model alone made acceptance stricter than apply, and an argument built over more than one staging call unacceptable by construction. Accept and Reject live in the Review panel, which shows why a change set cannot be accepted before the user reaches for the button rather than reporting it to the status bar afterwards; there is no tool an agent can call to apply its own work. Replaces the earlier design in which the adapter wrote proposal files into the project, making it a second writer of `af.proj` and `review-items.af.json` that the application overwrote from its own older copy on the next save. Known limit: when a change set is drawn, the canvas places a staged addition on the argument package it is connected to, and one connected to nothing goes on the first package; applying it puts every element on the first package regardless, because `RebuildSacmArgumentPackageFromParser` collapses them — pre-existing and shared with the interactive proposal flow, tracked separately.

features.name: SCCG guidance and checks for an external AI client
features.notes: Three mechanisms. **Resources**: `sccg://guidelines` publishes the catalog over MCP. **Prompts**: `draft_argument_from_standard`, `add_argumentation` and `restructure_case` each carry the guidance for that job, quoted from the catalog so prompt and guideline cannot drift — this is what makes an agent aware of the rules before it writes. **Checks**: findings returned in the result of every staging call and shown on the change set in the Review panel. The reviewer's half of that was claimed before it worked: the panel had the section and nothing ever filled the row it renders from, so only the agent ever saw a finding. The mechanical set is deliberately narrow and individually tested — EV.1 (claim with no support and no undeveloped marker), AR.2 (strategy developing into nothing), AR.1 (solution with children; support cycles), CL.5 (unbounded qualifier from the list SCCG names). Most of SCCG is prose only a reader can judge, so this is **not** "SCCG compliance": findings are advisory and never block acceptance.

features.name: Suggest where new argument belongs
features.notes: `suggest_placement(topic)` returns ranked goals and strategies with the path from the top goal, the sub-claims already there and the context in scope. Substring search says where a word appears, which is a different question from where an argument belongs; without this an agent guesses and attaches at the root. Ranked by term overlap and structural fit, not by understanding — the reply says so, and says to report that nothing fits rather than pick the best of a bad set. Only goals and strategies are offered as anchors.

features.name: Atomic re-parent for restructuring (`MoveUnder`)
features.notes: Restructuring is expressible today as remove-then-add supported-by pairs, so the capability exists, but a large restructure reads as a pile of unrelated operations and the intent is lost in the diff a reviewer has to approve. A `MoveUnder` patch operation would carry the intent atomically. Adding a `PatchOperationType` is backward compatible for reading existing audit logs. Not built.

features.name: Standards-clause traceability on claims
features.notes: An agent applying a standard records which clause a claim answers in the claim description, because the element model has no citation field. That is a trace a human can read but not one a tool can follow, filter or check for coverage. A first-class citation would be a SACM modelling decision, not an MCP one.
